talks.title: LT13
talks.teaser: Shows two hunting approaches for the MintLoader malware loader: patterns in its obfuscated JavaScript and its redirect domains.
talks.summary:
MintLoader is a two-stage loader. The first stage is heavily obfuscated JavaScript and the second is obfuscated PowerShell, and it is usually delivered through ClickFix-style lures. The speaker said it has been seen since early 2023 and that its samples use several URL patterns, some built around a recognizable name and others made of plain numbers. A typical infection chain was walked through to set up the rest of the talk.

The first hunting method focuses on the JavaScript itself. The speaker explained why the script contains an odd mix of church and Scotland related words and randomly capitalized terms: comments and some identifiers draw on a specific book, and capitalized words follow the chapter headings in that text. Once that pattern is understood, a simple search for JavaScript containing the same kinds of terms can surface more samples.

The second method looks at infrastructure. Searching for recently registered domains can reveal sites that redirect to randomly generated domains of a fixed length that are not registered. The speaker said many operators expose this behavior, and that several of these pages were hosted with one provider. The talk closed by presenting both techniques as new ways to track MintLoader infrastructure.

talks.title: LT10
talks.teaser: Demonstrates an LLM pipeline that turns a spoken request into a script producing network traffic captures.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a short prototype in which an AI model generates network traffic on request. The speaker explains the uses: building packet captures for testing, supporting malware work, checking Snort rules during QA, and simply making the idea fun. Several generation approaches were weighed, including writing Python code that crafts packets, or a more involved setup where a model switches live packet capture on and off. The speaker chose a tool whose human-readable intermediate language describes traffic and renders it as a pcap.

The pipeline works in stages. A spoken request is converted to text by a speech model, then passed to GPT-4o together with a prompt that explains the language, its syntax and examples, and formatting instructions. The model writes a script in that language, which runs in Docker and produces the capture. The live demo produced a DNS query and response for snort.org, and an HTTP request and response were shown as an example script.

To finish, the speaker suggested that the voice input is impractical and could be dropped. A retrieval-augmented generation layer supplying detailed protocol instructions could improve output for whichever protocol is being generated.

talks.title: LT2
talks.teaser: An IR case study unpacks SmokeHam from a fake RV Tools installer through registry-staged payloads to encrypted headless malware.
talks.summary:
At the end of 2024, an incident response team investigated ransomware tied to an international affiliate. Initial access came from an administrator who installed a counterfeit RV Tools package that dropped SmokeHam, a PowerShell backdoor delivered through a Nullsoft installer script and launched via DLL sideloading beside a legitimate view.exe. Attackers moved laterally and deployed ESXi ransomware across hundreds of hypervisors.

Weeks later, hunting turned up a fresh SmokeHam installer. Automated analysis pulled the malicious Nullsoft script, confirming the backdoor and run-key persistence. Running the sample in an isolated environment showed command-and-control through Cloudflare Workers. After further observation, the implant captured desktop screenshots to AWS, retrieved a payload from a Russian Proton66 host, hid it in an encoded registry value, and masqueraded as a Microsoft Edge update scheduled task that fired every two hours.

The staged PowerShell was simplified with a deobfuscation tool without execution, then decrypted and reflectively loaded a final headless PE module. That stage decrypts each function immediately before use, communicates over DNS tunneling, and exposes shell, file-blur, and shellcode-blur capabilities while removing its persistence. Practitioners gain a concrete picture of installer abuse, hunting payoff, staged C2, and anti-analysis in a post-ransomware intrusion.

talks.title: LT 10
talks.teaser: Shows how a conference stream controller uses a mini video mixer, OBS, Stream Deck and Companion to start and stop talk streams.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who joined the conference stream team this year, describes the problem of streaming and recording a multi-track conference: each talk has to go live and be captured at the right moment, without unwanted recordings or crashes. The setup is built around a mini video mixer with hardware sound control, OBS on a PC feed for scene handling, a Stream Deck for physical buttons, and YouTube Studio for setting up the live events.

Each talk gets its own stream key, and the stream goes live when that key is active. Companion software ties the devices together. The Stream Deck offers three main buttons. One changes talk and runs four actions at once: it stops recording and streaming, loads the configuration for the next talk, and puts the screen into a waiting mode showing the schedule. Another starts the talk by switching the scene to the speaker's PC and starting the conference feed when the speaker begins, with recording and YouTube streaming started if the talk is scheduled for them. The speaker also showed a photo of the device layout.

Companion also disables mixer buttons that are not valid for the current presentation, so nobody can start a stream or recording by mistake. The takeaway is that a schedule-driven setup with hardware controls removes many manual steps from live event streaming. The speaker closed by pointing to a blog post with more detail and offering to answer questions afterwards.

talks.title: LT1
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate LT1 and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Jerome from Nokia Deepfield shares insights into current and emerging Denial of Service (DoS) security threats. He addresses the shift in Nokia's core focus toward network infrastructure and routers, explaining how his day-to-day research tracks DoS activity using customer telemetry, internet-wide scanning, and active proxy discovery.

### Key Topics
- **DoS Threat Landscape**: For roughly the past five years, botnets have driven the majority of DoS attacks, currently generating about 60% of DoS traffic.
- **Botnet Composition**: Compromised devices historically include MikroTik routers, DVRs, unexpected connected systems such as parking meters in Korea, and exposed Jupyter notebooks exploited to launch DoS attacks against Minecraft servers.
- **Rise of Residential Proxies**: An emerging shift over the prior six months shows significant overlap between volumetric DoS source IP addresses and residential proxy nodes.
- **Scale and Detection Challenges**: Residential proxies are harder to discover because they often lack open ports for direct crawling, yet they represent a footprint orders of magnitude larger than traditional botnets.

### Technical Details
- **Data Sources and Discovery**: Research relies on customer telemetry (specifically NetFlow data), active IPv4 crawling to map devices and running services, and active residential proxy discovery.
- **Traditional Botnet Footprint**: Known DoS botnets account for approximately 1 million nodes, with individual attacks typically drawing from tens of thousands of source IPs.
- **Proxy Scale and BudBox**: Residential proxies, such as Badbox pre-installed at the factory on Android TV boxes, reach an estimated 100 million nodes—two orders of magnitude larger than standard botnets. Daily tracking observes approximately 30 million of these nodes, and attack sizes can involve significantly higher volumes of source IPs.
- **Discovery Hurdles**: Unlike traditional bots that expose open ports, residential proxy nodes generally do not accept direct inbound crawls, demanding active discovery methods.

### Takeaways
Volumetric DoS attacks are rapidly converging with residential proxy infrastructure, drastically increasing potential attack scale and obfuscation. Nokia Deepfield is actively collaborating across the industry to address the monitoring and mitigation challenges posed by these massive proxy networks. Note: The transcript cuts off mid-sentence during the concluding remarks.
